blocks.text: Apache Spark is a distributed processing engine: it turns one data program into coordinated work across many machines.
The problem Spark solves

A single computer eventually runs out of memory, CPU, or time. Vertical scaling buys a larger machine; horizontal scaling divides work across a cluster. Spark handles that division, schedules it, retries failures, and combines the results behind familiar APIs.

items.title: Scale out
items.text: Partitions let many CPU cores process separate pieces of a dataset concurrently.

items.title: Keep a plan
items.text: A directed acyclic graph preserves the dependency path between every operation.

items.title: Use one engine
items.text: Batch, SQL, streaming, machine learning, and graph workloads share one runtime.

blocks.text: Spark compared with MapReduce

blocks.title: Mental model
blocks.text: Spark is not a storage system. It reads from systems such as object storage, HDFS, Kafka, and databases, then coordinates computation.

items: Spark scales one logical computation across a cluster.
Its DAG execution model supports more than a rigid map/reduce pipeline.
Distributed speed depends on partitioning, movement, and scheduling—not only more machines.

blocks.text: Every Spark application is a conversation between a driver that plans, a manager that allocates, and executors that calculate.

blocks.caption: The driver plans work; the cluster manager allocates resources; executors run tasks and store data.

blocks.text: Responsibilities

head: Component
Owns
Failure impact
rows: Your main program, query plans, jobs, task scheduling
CPU and memory allocation across applications
The host process or machine for executors

blocks.text: SparkSession and SparkContext
**SparkSession** is the modern entry point for DataFrame, SQL, and streaming work. Underneath it, **SparkContext** connects the driver to the cluster and coordinates lower-level execution.

blocks.title: Isolation
blocks.text: Each Spark application receives its own executors. Separate applications do not share executor memory unless data is written to an external system.

items: The driver is the brain, not a data worker.
Executors live for the application and run many tasks over time.
Size driver and executor resources for their different responsibilities.

blocks.text: Spark is cluster-manager agnostic. The manager decides where processes run; Spark decides what those processes compute.

head: Manager
Best fit
Trade-off
rows: Easy to operate, fewer ecosystem controls
Development and tests on one machine

blocks.code:
# Standalone cluster
spark-submit --master spark://host:7077 app.py

# YARN
spark-submit --master yarn --deploy-mode cluster app.py

# Kubernetes
spark-submit --master k8s://https://cluster:6443 app.py

blocks.title: Choose for operations
blocks.text: The same DataFrame code can run on each manager. Choose from your platform, security, monitoring, elasticity, and team skills—not from API differences.

items: The cluster manager allocates processes; it does not create Spark's execution plan.
YARN fits Hadoop estates; Kubernetes fits container platforms.
Local mode is useful for learning but hides network and scale behavior.

blocks.text: Deploy mode answers one precise question: where does the driver process run?

items.label: Client mode
items.title: Driver stays with the submitter
items.text: Useful for notebooks, shells, and interactive debugging. The client must remain connected and reachable by executors.

items.label: Cluster mode
items.title: Driver runs inside the cluster
items.text: Preferred for scheduled production jobs because the submitter can disconnect after submission.

blocks.text: Network rule
Executors must communicate directly with the driver. In client mode, firewalls, VPNs, or a laptop sleeping can terminate an otherwise healthy job.

items: Deploy mode locates the driver; master selects the resource manager.
Use client mode for interactive work and cluster mode for production.
Driver reachability is a first-class architecture requirement.

lessons.title: From code to an execution plan

blocks.text: Spark does not execute each transformation immediately. It records intent, optimizes the whole plan, and starts only when an action demands a result.

items: User code
Logical plan
Optimized plan
Physical plan
Tasks

blocks.text: Lazy evaluation

blocks.code:
events = spark.read.parquet("s3://lake/events")
paid = events.filter("status = 'paid'")  # plan only
by_day = paid.groupBy("event_date").count()  # plan only
by_day.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("s3://lake/daily")  # action

blocks.text: The read, filter, and aggregation become a logical plan. The write is an action, so Spark chooses physical operators, divides the plan at shuffle boundaries, and sends tasks to executors.
Catalyst and whole-stage code generation

For SQL and DataFrames, Catalyst applies rules such as predicate pushdown, column pruning, constant folding, and join reordering. The physical plan then chooses operators such as broadcast hash join or sort-merge join.

blocks.title: Inspect before running
blocks.text: `df.explain("formatted")` reveals the logical and physical plans. It is often the fastest way to understand why data moved.

items: Transformations build plans; actions trigger jobs.
Catalyst can optimize structured operations because it understands schema and expressions.
The physical plan reveals exchanges, joins, scans, and filters.

blocks.text: Spark turns a high-level action into a hierarchy of increasingly small units of work.

head: Unit
Created by
Meaning
rows: All work for a submitted program
Work required to return or save one result
Tasks that can run without redistributing data
Smallest scheduled unit, run by one executor core

blocks.text: Narrow and wide dependencies

items.title: Narrow
items.text: Each output partition reads from a small number of input partitions. map and filter can pipeline in one stage.

items.title: Wide
items.text: Output partitions need data from many inputs. joins, groupBy, distinct, and repartition usually shuffle.

items: One action creates one or more jobs.
Wide dependencies create shuffle boundaries and new stages.
Partition count controls the number of tasks in a stage.

blocks.text: An RDD is an immutable, partitioned collection whose lineage records how every partition can be rebuilt.

items: Source RDD
map
filter
reduceByKey
Result

blocks.text: Three properties

items.title: Distributed
items.text: Partitions are processed concurrently on executors.

items.title: Immutable
items.text: A transformation creates a new RDD rather than changing the old one.

items.title: Resilient
items.text: Lost partitions can be recomputed from their lineage.

blocks.code:
lines = sc.textFile("s3://logs/*.txt")
errors = lines.filter(lambda line: "ERROR" in line)
counts = errors.map(lambda line: (line.split()[0], 1)) \
               .reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b)
print(counts.take(10))

blocks.text: Transformations and actions

head: Type
Examples
Behavior
rows: Triggers execution and returns or writes a result

blocks.title: Avoid collect
blocks.text: Calling `collect()` moves the entire result to driver memory. Use `take()`, write to storage, or aggregate first.

items: RDD lineage enables fault recovery without eagerly copying every partition.
Transformations are lazy; actions trigger computation.
Prefer structured APIs unless low-level control is genuinely required.

blocks.text: A DataFrame adds schema and expressions to distributed data, giving Spark enough information to optimize the work.

head: API
Strength
Use when
rows: Default for Python, Scala, Java, and R
DataFrame optimization plus JVM type safety
Fine-grained objects and custom partition logic
The structured APIs cannot express the computation
Analysts and transformations fit relational operations

blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

result = (spark.read.parquet("s3://lake/orders")
  .filter(F.col("status") == "paid")
  .groupBy("country")
  .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("revenue"))
  .orderBy(F.desc("revenue")))

result.explain("formatted")

blocks.text: Why DataFrames are usually faster

Spark can prune unused columns, push filters toward the source, select a join strategy, generate compact JVM code, and use efficient columnar formats. A raw Python RDD hides much of that intent behind arbitrary functions.

items: DataFrame is the default abstraction for modern Spark work.
Schema allows Spark to optimize before execution.
SQL and DataFrame code share the same Catalyst planning engine.

blocks.text: A shuffle redistributes records between executors. It is often the most expensive boundary in a Spark job.

blocks.label: shuffle write ↓ network fetch ↓ shuffle read

blocks.text: What causes one
Operations including **groupBy**, **distinct**, most joins, **orderBy**, and **repartition** require records with matching keys to meet in the same output partition.

head: Symptom
Likely cause
First response
rows: Salt the key or enable AQE skew handling
Filter and project before grouping or joining
Coalesce or let AQE combine partitions

blocks.code:
# Make a small dimension local to each executor
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
result = facts.join(broadcast(dim_customer), "customer_id")

# Inspect current parallelism
print(result.rdd.getNumPartitions())

items: A shuffle uses network, disk, serialization, and often sorting.
Filter early and avoid moving columns you do not need.
Partition count and data distribution matter more than a single magic number.

blocks.text: Caching trades executor memory for avoided recomputation. It helps only when the same expensive result is reused.

head: Storage level
Behavior
Typical use
rows: Keep deserialized partitions; recompute evicted data
Fast iterative reuse when memory is ample
Spill partitions that do not fit
Safer default for large reused datasets

blocks.text: Unified memory

Executor memory is shared between execution work—joins, sorts, aggregation—and storage for cached blocks. Execution can evict cached data. When either cannot fit, Spark spills to disk or fails if overhead exceeds the container limit.

blocks.title: Cache deliberately
blocks.text: Caching data used once adds work: materialization, memory pressure, and possible spill. Check the Storage tab and unpersist when reuse ends.

items: Cache reused, expensive results—not every DataFrame.
MEMORY_AND_DISK avoids repeated recomputation when data exceeds memory.
Unpersist finished datasets to free executor storage.

blocks.text: Spark expects machines and tasks to fail. The scheduler retries work and uses lineage to reconstruct lost data.

items: Task fails
Executor lost
Scheduler retries
Lineage rebuilds
Stage completes

blocks.text: Recovery at each layer

head: Failure
What Spark can do
What you control
rows: Make code deterministic and fix bad records
Run tasks elsewhere; rebuild cached partitions
Fix skew before relying on speculation
Use cluster mode and platform restart policies

blocks.text: FIFO and FAIR scheduling
Within one SparkContext, FIFO runs jobs in submission order by default. FAIR scheduling divides resources among pools so shorter or interactive work can progress alongside long jobs.

blocks.title: Exactly once is broader than Spark
blocks.text: A retried task may execute user code more than once. Avoid side effects inside transformations, and use idempotent or transactional output patterns.

items: Lineage repairs data partitions; task retry repairs computation.
Driver failure is different from executor failure.
Retries make side effects dangerous unless writes are idempotent.

lessons.title: Read the Spark UI & diagnose jobs

blocks.text: The Spark UI turns an abstract DAG into evidence: where time went, where bytes moved, and which executor struggled.
A repeatable diagnostic sequence

items: Open the SQL or Jobs tab and locate the slow action.
Find the longest stage in the DAG.
Compare median and maximum task duration to detect skew.
Check shuffle read/write, input size, spill, and garbage-collection time.
Open Executors to identify one unhealthy host or uneven task distribution.
Map the physical operator back to the relevant source transformation.

head: Signal
Interpretation
Likely fix
rows: Reduce partition size or tune resources
Use DataFrames, reduce caching, right-size heap
AQE, salting, or different partition key
Compact files and tune file partition sizing
Too much data returned to driver

items: Start with the longest stage, then inspect task distribution.
Shuffle, spill, GC, and skew each leave distinct evidence.
Use the plan and UI together: one explains structure, the other shows runtime cost.

lessons.title: Capstone: optimize a slow Spark job

blocks.text: Bring the architecture together by diagnosing a slow customer-revenue pipeline before changing any configuration.
The scenario
A daily pipeline joins 1.2 billion transaction rows to a 40 MB customer table, groups by country, and writes 2,000 tiny files. One stage lasts 28 minutes while most tasks finish in 40 seconds.
Evidence before tuning

head: Observation
Inference
rows: Spark did not broadcast the small dimension
One key or partition is heavily skewed
Too much data crossed the network

blocks.text: A reasoned revision

blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast

result = (transactions
  .select("customer_id", "amount")
  .join(broadcast(customers.select("customer_id", "country")), "customer_id")
  .groupBy("country")
  .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("revenue"))
  .coalesce(8))

result.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("s3://curated/revenue")

blocks.title: Measure again
blocks.text: A code change is a hypothesis. Compare total duration, shuffle bytes, spill, task distribution, and file sizes after every revision.
Production checklist

items: Filter and select columns before joins and aggregations.
Confirm join choice with `explain("formatted")`.
Use AQE, but understand what it changed.
Watch maximum task time, not only the average.
Control output files without collapsing a large workload to one partition.
Capture Spark UI event logs for later comparison.

blocks.label: Continue learning
blocks.text: Use the official Apache Spark documentation as the source of truth for behavior and configuration in your installed version.

items: Diagnose from evidence before adding resources or configuration.
Reduce data early, broadcast genuinely small inputs, and control output partitions.
Optimization is a measured loop: plan, observe, change, compare.
